records.name_note: Sources converge on "Loblolly Pine" as the lead common name for Pinus taeda specifically (not P. strobus, P. echinata, or P. palustris). NC State's Common Name(s) field carries three alphabetized entries -- Loblolly Pine, Oldfield Pine, Yellow Pine -- whose first entry is Loblolly Pine, and NC State's body prose leads with "Loblolly pine" both in its opening description and in its culture paragraph. MoBot's Common Name field independently displays the single value "loblolly pine" (a longer seven-name list exists only inside the tooltip link's overlib attribute markup, so it is not quoted here). RHS renders "loblolly pine" as the plant-profile subtitle under the heading Pinus taeda, and lists "old field pine" among its Other common names, echoing NC State's "Oldfield Pine".
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail left null: none of the admissible sources (NC State, Clemson HGIC, MoBot, UF/IFAS, RHS) report a Poison block or any cat/dog-scoped toxicity for Pinus taeda; NC State's page carries no Poison Part/Poison Severity fields and no 'Poisonous' or 'Poisonous to Humans' tag in its Plant Type or Problems listings.

chill_damage_f/cool_rest_note left null: MoBot states 'Hardy to around Zones 6b (-5-0°F)', which is a hardiness-zone survival rating, not a stated damage-onset temperature; no admissible source gives a literal onset figure.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no source states daytime/nighttime temperature preferences; only USDA hardiness zone ranges are given (NC State 6a-9b, UF/IFAS 6B-9B, MoBot Zone 6-9), which are zone ratings, not day/night temperature fields.

humidity_need and humidity_pct_min/max left null: no source states a humidity requirement; MoBot and NC State both say only that the tree "performs best in climates with hot and humid summers and mild winters", which is a regional-climate suitability statement (and NC State's culture paragraph closely tracks MoBot's, so it is not independent corroboration).

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max left null: no species-specific footcandle or sun-hour figure was found; NC State's '6 or more hours' text is the site-wide Full Sun legend definition rather than species-specific prose, so per instructions it was not used to populate direct_sun_hours_max.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's Soil pH field for this species reads only the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band, which sets no floor or ceiling per instructions, and the fetched RHS species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/44706/pinus-taeda/details) carries no pH field to cross-check in either direction.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis left null: Loblolly pine is an in-ground landscape tree and no admissible source frames its watering as a dry-down or day-interval schedule.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength left null: none of the admissible sources give a fertilizing schedule, timing, or dilution strength for Pinus taeda; Clemson's factsheet is a multi-species pine factsheet with no species-specific fertilizer program, and none was found on NC State, MoBot, UF/IFAS, or RHS.

A WebSearch snippet claimed a 'medium-low' hurricane resistance rating for loblolly pine from Clemson HGIC, but the fetched page text shows that wind-tolerance language applies only to longleaf pine, not loblolly pine, so it was not used anywhere in this record.

Clemson HGIC's 'Pine' factsheet is a multi-species publication, not a dedicated single-species page, and was used only for corroborating prose (growth rate, soil adaptability, acid-soil preference), consistent with the instruction not to treat it as a lead-naming source.

water_regime was nulled at landing: the record's keep_moist rested on MoBot's "Prefers moist, acidic soils with poor drainage." and its structured "Water: Medium to wet", with NC State's "Grow Loblolly pine in medium to wet soils and in full sun." -- soil-moisture site descriptors for an in-ground tree, not a watering statement, which is what this catalog requires for a regime (the same rule that kept Ohio Buckeye's 'Prefers moist, fertile soils' out of water_regime in b65). All three are disclosed here.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's page — titled Picea laxa, with Picea glauca listed under 'Previously known as' — gives eight Common Name(s) entries (Black Hills Spruce, Canada Spruce, Cat Spruce, Porslid Spruce, Single Spruce, Skunk Spruce, Western White Spruce, White Spruce), in alphabetical order and matching the page-title parenthetical. RHS's dedicated page for Picea glauca gives 'white spruce' in its title and subtitle, and MoBot's Common Name field, a single rendered value, reads 'Common Name: white spruce'. White Spruce is used on that basis; NC State's seven other names are carried as unranked alternates.
unknowns: Confirmed straight-species identity before use: NC State's page (title 'Picea laxa (Black Hills Spruce, Canada Spruce, Cat Spruce, Porslid Spruce, Single Spruce, Skunk Spruce, Western White Spruce, White Spruce) | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox') lists Picea glauca under 'Previously known as:'; MoBot's page title read 'Picea glauca  - Plant Finder' after correcting an initial mis-redirect; RHS's page title read 'Picea glauca | white spruce' with URL slug /plants/12941/picea-glauca/details. All three are the straight species, not the 'Conica'/'Densata' dwarf Alberta spruce cultivar pages.

toxic_to_pets / toxicity_detail left null: none of the three admissible sources (NC State, MoBot, RHS) mention toxicity to cats, dogs, or any other animal for this species, and NC State's Plant Type list carries no 'Poisonous' tag and its Problems/tags carry no poison-related entries.

chill_damage_f / cool_rest_note left null: no source states a cold-damage onset temperature. This is a cold-hardy species (NC State lists USDA Plant Hardiness Zones 2a-6b) rather than a cold-sensitive one, so a chill-damage figure would not be expected; the species is instead heat-sensitive (see heat/scorch note below), for which the schema has no dedicated field.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max left null: no source gives explicit degree-Fahrenheit day or night temperature ranges; only USDA hardiness zone data is available, which per instructions is not a substitute for stated temperature figures.

Heat/exposure warnings captured here since no schema field fits them: NC State's Description states 'It grows in cool climates, cannot tolerate hot, humid summers.' and 'Air circulation is important to rid the dense foliage of excess moisture.'; its Problems sentence separately notes the species is 'one of the most tolerant spruces for wind, heat, cold, drought, and crowding' (a same-source, non-contradictory note about relative tolerance among spruces, not a reversal of the hot-humid-summer intolerance). MoBot's Culture section states 'Best performance is in cold winter climates with cool summers... Plants will struggle in the high heat and humidity of St. Louis summers, and should not be grown in the eastern U.S. south of USDA Zone 6.'

NC State's structured Light field also lists 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', and MoBot's Culture prose adds 'Tolerates some light shade.' Both are tolerance statements; MoBot's and RHS's structured sun fields list only full sun, so part_shade is disclosed here rather than carried into outdoor_sun_exposure.

soil_ph_min/max left null: NC State's plant page for this species carries no Soil pH field at all. RHS's pH field gives only the qualitative descriptor 'Acid or Neutral' with no numeric bounds stated, so no numeric ceiling or floor could be derived per the instructions.

water_regime and the water_* fields left null: no source gives a species-specific watering statement. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium', which per instructions is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist; it is noted here only as a disclosed, non-adopted data point. This is also an in-ground landscape tree, so the day-interval and dry-down-target fields are left null absent any source framing watering that way.
fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength left null: no admissible source provides any fertilizer guidance for this species.

light_fc_min/good and direct_sun_hours_max left null: no source gives foot-candle figures, and NC State's '6 or more hours' figure comes from its site-wide light-category legend rather than species-specific prose, so per instructions it was not used for direct_sun_hours_max.
humidity_need and humidity_pct_min/max left null: none of the three sources address humidity requirements for this outdoor tree.

soil_drainage is moderate on RHS's 'Moist but well–drained' and MoBot's 'Best grown in moist, well-drained soils'; NC State's structured Soil Drainage field (Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry, Very Dry) is a wider band that includes the moderate reading and extends to very dry, disclosed here rather than mapped.

Clemson HGIC's factsheet is titled "Sweetshrub" and lists Carolina allspice among other common names: "Sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus) has many common names, including Carolina allspice, strawberry-bush, sweet bubby, sweet Betsy, and spicebush." records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block for Calycanthus floridus is scoped to humans (its own tag reads 'Poisonous to Humans'), rating Poison Severity as 'Low', Poison Symptoms as 'Convulsions, elevated blood pressure', Poison Toxic Principle as 'Calycanthin and related alkaloids', and Poison Part as 'Seeds', with Causes Contact Dermatitis recorded as 'No'. This sits alongside NC State's Plant Type tags of Native Plant, Perennial, Poisonous, Shrub. No Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tags appear anywhere on the NC State page. Clemson HGIC's Sweetshrub factsheet adds a dosage caveat not present in NC State's Poison block: 'The seeds are poisonous, but only if eaten in large quantities.' Neither admissible source names cats or dogs specifically, so this evidence supports general/human toxicity but not a cat/dog-scoped determination. RHS's profile for Calycanthus floridus adds a hazard line neither NC State nor Clemson carries — "Humans/Pets: Harmful if eaten. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling" — which supplies a handling warning and scopes the hazard to humans and pets rather than humans alone. RHS's unqualified "Harmful if eaten" also sits against NC State's Poison Part of "Seeds" and Clemson's "The seeds are poisonous, but only if eaten in large quantities"; the sources disagree on how much of the plant is hazardous and at what dose. RHS names "Pets" without naming cats or dogs, so it still cannot scope a cat/dog determination.

records.name_note: Sources split on both the common name and which binomial is currently accepted. NC State's page title and stacked Common Name(s) field carry the same eleven entries in alphabetical order (Bayberry, Candleberry, Dwarf Bayberry, Dwarf Wax-myrtle, Eastern Bayberry, Southern Bayberry, Southern Waxmyrtle, Southern Wax Myrtle, Tallow Shrub, Waxmyrtle, Wax Myrtle), so first position there reflects alphabetization rather than a preferred name; NC State's own description opens "Wax myrtle is a broadleaf evergreen shrub or tree in the bayberry family (Myricaceae) that may grow 20 to 25 feet tall and 8 to 10 feet wide, but usually is much shorter.", which is the common_name value used here. NC State's "Previously known as" field reads "Morella cerifera", i.e. that page treats Myrica cerifera as the name currently in use. Missouri Botanical Garden's page, headed Morella cerifera, shows a single Common Name field value "wax myrtle" and states in its Noteworthy Characteristics "Myrica cerifera is a synonym." Clemson HGIC's Waxmyrtle factsheet (HGIC 1076), whose main entry is Morella cerifera and which also carries a Related Species section on M. pumila, M. pensylvanica and M. caroliniensis, agrees: "Common waxmyrtle or Southern bayberry (Morella cerifera; formerly Myrica cerifera) is native to South Carolina and other southeastern States." RHS's page is titled "Myrica cerifera | southern bayberry", subtitles the plant southern bayberry, lists "wax myrtle" only under Other common names ("bayberry, candleberry, tallow myrtle, tallow shrub, wax myrtle"), and its Name status field reads "Synonym". Because MoBot and Clemson both state that Myrica cerifera is the former/synonym name and Morella cerifera the current one, scientific_name_accepted is set to Morella cerifera; NC State's contrary framing is disclosed here as an unresolved conflict rather than adopted.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot, Clemson, RHS) carries a Poison block, a Problems-for-Cats/Dogs tag, or any other statement about toxicity to animals or humans for this species; NC State's Plant Type field does not include 'Poisonous' and its Problems tags do not include 'Poisonous to Humans'. Left null rather than guessed.

Fire/flammability: not a schema field, but captured here per instructions. NC State (structured Fire Risk Rating: 'high flammability') and its body prose: 'Fire Risk: These shrubs are considered to be potential fire hazards in some areas because the leaves, stems and branches contain flammable aromatic compounds. Because of this, they should not be planted within the defensible space of your home. Select plants with a low flammability rating for the sites nearest your home.' Missouri Botanical Garden's page carries the same statement in its Noteworthy Characteristics prose: 'These shrubs are considered to be potential fire hazards in some areas because the leaves, stems and branches contain flammable aromatic compounds.' Clemson HGIC's factsheet contains no fire/flammability statement.

soil_ph: NC State's structured Soil pH field reads only the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', which per the rules cannot set a ceiling or floor. RHS's page for this species has no Soil/pH field at all (it is a sparse synonym-status stub with only Family, Native to GB/Ireland, Genus, and Name Status populated), so there is no RHS pH field to cross-check against. Clemson notes 'Iron chlorosis (yellowing of the leaf tissue between the veins) is a problem in high pH soils' as a qualitative warning but gives no numeric ceiling. Left both soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max null.

water_regime: no source frames watering for this in-ground shrub in keep_moist/dry_surface_between terms. MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium to wet' (mid-scale, disclosed as a counterpoint per the rules, not adopted). MoBot's culture prose ('Best initially grown with constant moisture, but once established in the landscape it will grow in a wide range of soil conditions ranging from wet swampy areas to dry xeric uplands') and NC State's near-identical prose describe an establishment-vs-established distinction that does not map cleanly onto a single enum value, so left null.

RHS's Myrica cerifera page (https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/11294/myrica-cerifera/details) was verified to match this species by both URL slug epithet and page title ('Myrica cerifera | southern bayberry') before use, per the admissibility check, but its Botanical Details are minimal (Family, blank Native to GB/Ireland, blank Genus value, and Name Status: Synonym only) - it carries no Position, Soil, or Cultivation sections to draw on.
